tour.title: French Concession Lanes
tour.summary: Tree-lined lanes of the old French district: a ship-shaped apartment block, a revolutionary widow's villa, cafe lanes, garden mansions and a plane-tree park to finish.
tour.overviewText:
Come to the corner where a ship-shaped apartment block points its prow down two tunnels of plane trees, and you are standing in the Shanghai that foreigners planted and locals made their own. This walk is your way through it, leaf by leaf.

This district matters because for nearly a century it was not quite China. After Britain forced Shanghai open in 1842, France took its own slice in 1849 and governed it as a concession — a district ruled by a foreign power — until it was handed back in 1946, and supporters of the old order called it orderly, green and modern while Chinese histories call it humiliation priced in rent; the trees hold both, and this tour states them and moves on. What the French left behind was a street plan of shady avenues and lilong — lane neighbourhoods of narrow alleys — lined with shikumen, the stone-gate houses named for the carved stone doorframes every family passed through. Behind those gates the lane life still runs: laundry lines, breakfast stalls, mahjong through open windows, aunties sweeping the same three metres of alley for thirty years. Outsiders get this district wrong by calling it Paris; it is Shanghai doing what Shanghai does, absorbing the foreign street and spending it locally.

That spending is the argument you will walk through. The villas that survived demolition now pour flat whites and sell knitwear, and the tension is one breath: newcomers call it revival, old residents call it rent, and both are standing in the same lane watching each other. Prices here are in RMB, meaning yuan (CNY), and the coffee costs what coffee costs in any rich city on earth.

The shape of the walk is a drift. You start at the great wedge of Wukang Mansion in the south, wander north up the plane-tree lanes of Wukang and Anfu Roads, then cruise the long eastern avenues to the garden mansions of Sinan Road and finish under the trees of Fuxing Park. About 5.9 km, roughly an hour and a quarter of actual walking, with one long leg in the middle that earns its coffee.

Come in December, when the plane trees stand bare and the lanes belong to residents again. Expect 5 to 10 degrees and damp air that feels colder than the number, because Shanghai has no city-wide central heating — so treat the heated cafes as warming stations, pick a hotel that states its heating plainly, and walk the middle of the day when the light lies sideways down the lanes. Mornings are the quiet window; weekends the cafes queue.

Bring small notes, look up at the balconies, and let the lanes set the pace. They always win.
tour.difficulty: Easy but long. About 5.9 km of flat city walking; the difficulty is one 2.6 km middle leg, narrow uneven lane paving, and thresholds at old doorways.
tour.bestTimeOfDay: Start around 10:00. In December the lanes are quietest on weekday mornings, the light runs sideways down Wukang Road by midday, and Fuxing Park fills with dancers and singers toward mid-afternoon.
tour.imageCredits: Photographs are bundled from Wikimedia Commons under public domain or Creative Commons licences. Individual credits appear under each stop's photograph.

stops.name: Wukang Mansion
stops.entranceFeeNote: Exterior only; people live here. The ground-floor shops price in RMB (CNY). No ticket; verify nothing, just look.
stops.openingHours: Open access daily from the pavement. The corner photographs best in morning light; the shops keep roughly 10:00 to 22:00 hours.
stops.accessibility: Flat wide pavements at the corner, step free. Do not enter the residential stairwells; the interior is not a sight.
stops.insiderTip: Cross to the far corner of Huaihai Road and frame the prow head-on: the wedge reads as a ship only from dead ahead, with a plane tree on each side like masts.
stops.nextStopDirections: Cross Huaihai Road to the north side, about 180 metres, roughly 3 minutes. The grey villa with the garden wall just east of the corner is the next stop.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: N509FZ, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
stops.narration:
Stop at the corner and look at the ship that never sails. Wukang Mansion rises in a brick wedge, narrow prow aimed down the junction, balconies curving like decks — raised in 1924 as the Normandie Apartments by a French developer, when this whole district was a concession, meaning a slice of the city governed by France rather than China. The French ran their own council, police and plane-tree planting here from 1849 until the district was handed back in 1946, and this block was their postcard: modern flats for foreign staff and rich Chinese tenants, with shops at the foot and servants in the attics.

The mechanism is tenancy as history. The film stars, writers and officials who rented here made the building famous enough that no developer has dared flatten it, and fame is the only preservation law that ever worked in Shanghai. People still live inside, so the lesson is a pavement one: exterior only, no stairwells, voices down. Browsing the ground-floor shops is free, prices in RMB, meaning yuan (CNY).

Cross to the far side of Huaihai Road and frame the prow head-on — the ship reads only from dead ahead. Then walk about 180 metres, roughly 3 minutes, to the grey villa with the garden wall just east of the corner. A revolutionary widow lived there.

stops.name: Soong Ching-ling Memorial Residence
stops.entranceFeeNote: Ticketed memorial: about ¥20 (CNY) at last check. Verify prices at the gate; Chinese house museums revise them.
stops.openingHours: Open roughly 09:00 to 16:30, closed Mondays at last check. Verify locally; the garden closes before the building.
stops.accessibility: Garden paths are level but the villa interior has stairs and narrow doorways; not step free inside. Wheelchair users get a fair visit from the garden and the ground-floor rooms.
stops.insiderTip: Ask for the English leaflet at the ticket window and read it in the garden first: the rooms make sense only once you know whose widow she was.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave by the gate, turn back past the mansion corner onto Wukang Road, and walk north about 670 metres, roughly 10 minutes, under the plane trees. The lane deepens as you go.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: SSYoung, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
stops.narration:
Step through the garden wall and the lane noise drops away. This grey villa at 1843 Huaihai Road was the home of Soong Ching-ling — Song Qingling — the widow of Sun Yat-sen, the revolutionary credited as the founder of modern China who toppled the last emperor in 1911. She lived here through war, occupation and revolution, and after 1949 the new government honoured her as an honorary leader while she quietly used the house to shelter friends the politics had stranded. Ticket about ¥20, meaning yuan (CNY), verify at the gate; closed Mondays at last check.

The mechanism is the widow's veto. Soong outlived every faction, refused to be owned by any of them, and her survival turned a private villa into neutral ground — the one address in Shanghai where enemies could each claim a friend. Walk the rooms slowly: the books, the plain desk, the photographs of her with foreign dignitaries she charmed into donations. Then stand in the garden she planted herself and notice the lesson the concession taught backwards: a French-built villa, owned by a Chinese revolutionary, preserved by a Communist state. Every regime found a use for her, and she found a use for every regime.

Blunt note: stairs and narrow doorways inside, no step-free route upstairs; the garden and ground floor carry the visit for wheels. Leave by the gate, turn back past the mansion corner onto Wukang Road, and walk north about 670 metres, roughly 10 minutes, under the plane trees.

stops.name: Wukang Road Plane-Tree Lanes
stops.entranceFeeNote: Open street. No ticket; the cafes and bookshops price in RMB (CNY). Verify menu prices as you go — this is the priciest coffee in Shanghai.
stops.openingHours: Open access daily. Mid-morning to midday gives the sideways light; the street never closes but the shops do, roughly 10:00 to 22:00.
stops.accessibility: Paved pavements, mostly level, but narrow with tree roots lifting the slabs in places. Step free with care; weekend crowds force single file.
stops.insiderTip: Walk the east pavement going north: the canopy is thickest there, and the villa gates and old lane mouths open on that side.
stops.nextStopDirections: Keep north to the top of the lane, then turn right onto Anfu Road and walk about 970 metres in all, roughly 15 minutes. The cafes thicken as the villas give way to shikumen lanes.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Livelikerw, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
stops.narration:
Now walk, and let the street do the teaching. Wukang Road runs north under a roof of plane trees — French platanes, planted by the French council a century ago because Paris had them and the concession wanted shade with status. The trunks fatten, the roots lift the paving slabs, and the canopy knits overhead so completely that summer here runs five degrees cooler than the avenue one block over. That is not decoration; it is climate infrastructure, planted by colonists and inherited by everyone.

Read the houses as you go. Behind the gates stand the villas of the 1920s and 30s — Spanish stucco beside Tudor brick beside French art deco — because the concession set few style rules and rich tenants built their home countries from memory. Below them run the lilong, the lane neighbourhoods, and their shikumen houses, named for the stone doorframes — stone-warehouse-gate — every family passed through. One street, two cities: villas for the rich, lanes for the clerks and tailors who served them, sharing the same trees.

Browsing is free; the coffee is the priciest in Shanghai, prices in RMB (yuan), so window-shop the menus first. Walk the east pavement north for the thickest canopy, then turn right onto Anfu Road: about 970 metres in all, roughly 15 minutes, as the villas give way to cafe lanes.

stops.name: Anfu Road Cafe Lane
stops.entranceFeeNote: Open lanes; browsing is free. Cafes and boutiques price in RMB (CNY); verify as you go — December menus add the heating surcharge of a second coffee.
stops.openingHours: Lanes open access daily. Shops roughly 10:00 to 22:00; weekday mornings are calm, weekends queue from late morning.
stops.accessibility: Narrow lanes, uneven stones, steps and thresholds at every old doorway; not step free and hard going for wheels.
stops.insiderTip: Look above the shop signs at the upper floors: the drying laundry and potted winter greens mark the flats where lane families still live over the espresso machines.
stops.nextStopDirections: This is the long leg: about 2.6 km, roughly 35 to 40 minutes on foot, heading east along the plane-tree avenues toward Sinan Road. Walk it — the avenues are the sight — or ride two metro stops if your feet vote otherwise.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Fayhoo, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
stops.narration:
Turn onto Anfu Road and the concession puts on its present-day costume. The shikumen lanes here — those stone-gate alleys you learned on Wukang Road — now trade as Shanghai's boutique strip: a 1930s lane house pours single-origin coffee, the next sells knitwear, the next frames prints. The bones are original — carved doorframes, timber stairs, courtyard wells — and the tenants are new, which is exactly the argument. Newcomers call it revival, old residents call it rent, and both are standing in the same alley watching each other; hold both, and spend where the making is visible.

Look above the shop signs while you sip. The upper floors still fly laundry lines and winter greens in pots, because lane families live over the espresso machines and hang their washing where the branding consultants would put a logo. That is the test of an honest lane: residents upstairs, commerce downstairs, neither having evicted the other yet. Browsing is free, prices in yuan, and in December a hot drink doubles as a hand warmer — Shanghai's damp cold finds every gap.

From here the walk stretches its legs. The next stop is about 2.6 km east, roughly 35 to 40 minutes on foot along the plane-tree avenues — Fuxing, Huaihai and Nanchang Roads — toward Sinan Road. Walk it, because the avenues are the sight: villa walls, corner bakeries, the whole eastern concession unspooling. Or ride two metro stops if your feet vote otherwise; no shame, and the totals on this tour count the walked line.

stops.name: Sinan Mansions
stops.entranceFeeNote: Open quarter; strolling is free. Restaurants price in RMB (CNY) at dinner levels — verify menus before sitting. The small memorial at No. 73 is free at last check; verify locally.
stops.openingHours: Courtyards open access daily. Restaurants roughly 11:00 to late; the No. 73 memorial keeps museum hours, roughly 09:00 to 16:30, closed Mondays at last check — verify locally.
stops.accessibility: Level paved courtyards, mostly step free. Individual villas have steps and thresholds; the memorial interior is tight.
stops.insiderTip: Find No. 73 on the west side: its small free memorial marks the house where the revolutionary organiser Zhou Enlai sheltered, and it is the quietest door in the quarter.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave by the south courtyard onto Fuxing Road and walk about 720 metres, roughly 10 minutes, east to the park gates. The trees ahead mean the finish.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: 钉钉, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
stops.narration:
Come out of the avenues into garden quiet. Sinan Mansions gathers some fifty 1920s and 30s garden villas — brick, stucco, blackwood staircases — into one strolling quarter, renovated in the 2010s instead of demolished, which in Shanghai counts as a fairy-tale ending. The mechanism is Expo money with taste: the city needed a face for 2010, bought the whole block's leases out, and rebuilt the villas as restaurants, offices and one honest memorial rather than a mall wearing a villa costume. Strolling is free, prices in yuan, and dinner here charges dinner prices, so check menus before the host seats you.

Find No. 73 on the west side. Its small memorial — free at last check, verify locally — marks the house where Zhou Enlai, the Communist organiser who became China's long-serving premier, sheltered and plotted in the 1940s under the foreigners' noses. That is the quarter in one door: a revolution organised from a French garden villa, then preserved by the state it produced.

One pass-note for lane collectors: Tianzifang, the lane warren covered in the Bund tour, sits about ten minutes south of here — add it if your feet agree, or bank it for another day. Otherwise leave by the south courtyard and walk about 720 metres, roughly 10 minutes, east along Fuxing Road. The trees ahead are the finish.

stops.name: Fuxing Park
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free public park. No ticket and no gate fee; verify nothing. Snack carts price in RMB (CNY).
stops.openingHours: Open daily, roughly 06:00 to 18:00 with seasonal shifts. Verify locally; mornings belong to the dancers, afternoons to everyone.
stops.accessibility: Level paved paths, the kindest walking of the day and largely step free. Benches throughout; the side grottoes have steps.
stops.insiderTip: Come for the mid-afternoon handover: the ballroom dancers pack up, the opera singers take the pavilions, and the plane-tree avenue in the middle holds the day's last light.
stops.nextStopDirections: End of the walk. Retrace the plane-tree avenue to the north gates, where taxis wait; Xintiandi's rebuilt lanes begin two blocks east if you want gloss after this, and South Huangpi Road metro station is about 10 minutes on foot.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Jpbowen, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
stops.narration:
Walk under the gates into the greenest acre of the old concession. Fuxing Park was laid out in 1909 as the French Park — the colonists' own pleasure ground of lawns, plane trees and a bandstand — and after 1949 it was renamed and handed to the people it had once excluded, which is why the statues by the gate now honour Marx and Engels instead of a governor. No ticket, free, open roughly 06:00 to 18:00 with the seasons; verify the board, and take the level paths, which are the easiest walking of your day.

The mechanism is the park as living room. Shanghai flats are small and grandparents mind the children, so every morning the lanes empty into here: tai chi at dawn, ballroom dancing by nine, opera singers holding pavilions by the afternoon, card games that outlast governments. Watch one dance circle right through a song. Nobody paid, nobody organised it, and everybody knows the steps — this is what the concession's trees were really for, though the French never guessed the dancers.

End of the walk. You started where a French wedge aimed its prow down the avenues, and you finish where the whole district comes to dance — same trees, same stubbornness, a century apart. Xintiandi's rebuilt lanes begin two blocks east if you want gloss after this; otherwise retrace the avenue to the north gates, where taxis wait and South Huangpi Road metro is about 10 minutes on foot. Go eat something — you have earned it.
